en: They live in a grand house.
note: English does not predicate wealth of a building; «бога́тый дом» is an opulent one, and "grand" is what a native speaker writes.

en: The sick girl was lying in bed.
note: English "ill" is predicative — someone is ill, but it is a sick child. The sibling sentence has the same problem.

en: The doctor examined the sick children.
note: Attributive "ill children" is not English; "sick" is the attributive form.

en: The adult daughter lives on her own.
note: "Lives separately" carries отде́льно across without translating it — the English for living apart from one's parents is "on her own".

en: He is already an adult.
note: "Adult person" is redundant: English "adult" is already the noun, so челове́к needs no separate word.

en: It was an evident mistake.
note: A mistake is not "visible" in English; ви́димый here is apparent rather than perceptible. "Evident" keeps it distinct from я́вный, glossed "obvious".

en: At the present moment I am busy.
note: "At the given moment" is not English, though "in the given case" (the sibling) is ordinary formal register.

en: I feel peace of mind.
note: "Heartfelt calm" is not a collocation English has; «душе́вное споко́йствие» is peace of mind.

en: She is wearing a gold ring.
note: English uses "gold" for the material and "golden" for the colour or the quality; a ring made of it is a gold ring.

en: They found gold coins.
note: Same as the ring: the material takes "gold".

en: He has a heart of gold.
note: «золото́й хара́ктер» is a set phrase and "a golden character" is not English. The English idiom for the same thing is a heart of gold.

en: They need financial help.
note: «материа́льная по́мощь» is money; "material help" reads as help made of matter.

en: They have financial difficulties.
note: Same false friend as the sibling — материа́льный about means is financial.

en: He is known internationally.
note: "At the world level" is the Russian phrase transliterated; English says internationally or worldwide.

en: He has an opinion of his own.
note: «осо́бое мне́ние» is a view that differs from everyone else's, which "a particular opinion" does not say.

en: Yet another crisis arrived.
note: очередно́й is not "next" in sequence but the latest in a wearying series, which "yet another" carries.

en: Yet another week began.
note: Same as the sibling: очередно́й marks one more of the same, not the one that comes next.

«Поверни́ на пра́вой стороне́» is not how the instruction is given — that is «поверни́ напра́во». The English inherits the oddity, and no rendering of this Russian will be natural. Needs the Russian fixed, which the annotation on this sentence puts out of reach of an automatic rewrite.
«за́ла» is an archaic feminine form of «зал» that a learner should not be shown as the ordinary word. The English is fine; the Russian is the half to fix.
«Така́я при́нятая фо́рма обще́ния» does not parse as a sentence — it wants «Э́то при́нятая фо́рма» or «Така́я фо́рма обще́ния при́нята». The stilted English inversion is downstream of that.

en: We worked on it together.
note: "We had joint work" is not a sentence English produces; the adjective belongs on the verb.

«солёные огурцы́» are pickled cucumbers, not salty ones — the salt is what preserves them, and no English speaker calls them salty. The other two sentences (salty soup, salty fish) use the sense the gloss covers, so this is the gloss being narrow rather than the sentence being wrong. Widening солёный to reach "pickled" is a decision for the gloss pass.

en: Appropriate measures were taken.
note: "Corresponding measures" asks what they correspond to; соотве́тствующий in this frame is "appropriate".

en: There are works of art in the museum.
note: "Artistic works" reads as works done artistically; худо́жественные рабо́ты in a museum are works of art.

en: He became calmer.
note: English forms the comparative of a two-syllable adjective in -m with -er, so "more calm" is ungrammatical here even though бо́лее is the Russian word being taught.

en: We need a quieter place.
note: Same as the sibling: "more quiet" is not the English comparative of quiet.

en: Nothing lasts forever.
note: "Lasts eternally" is not said; the fixed English is "nothing lasts forever".

en: He is always late for work.
note: ве́чно here is the exasperated "always", not a claim about eternity.

en: I will remember you forever.
note: "Remember eternally" is not English; forever is the word.

en: The bird flew up in fright.
note: "Fearfully" describes a manner of acting, which a bird taking off does not have; English puts the emotion in a prepositional phrase.

en: The audience gave a standing ovation.
note: "Applauded standing" is the Russian gerund carried across; the English for applauding on one's feet is a standing ovation.

ru: Она́ отвеча́ет, де́скать, э́то не её де́ло.
en: She answers that it is supposedly none of her business.
note: "That supposedly" stacks the two function words the wrong way round; the adverb belongs inside the clause.

ru: Он сказа́л, де́скать, у него́ не́ было вре́мени.
en: He said he supposedly had no time.
note: Same fix as the sibling, and the redundant "that" goes with it.

en: The children went on the ride.
note: The headword is glossed "ride" and its two sibling sentences say ride; only this one says "attraction", which is also not what an English speaker calls a fairground ride.

ru: Он за́нял пе́рвое ме́сто в бе́ге.
en: He took first place in the race.
note: "In the running" means something else entirely in English — still a contender — so the sentence reads as a joke.

en: They helped us when we were in trouble.
note: "In misfortune" is not an English adverbial; «в беде́» is being in trouble.

ru: Она́ обожа́ет пе́сни в сти́ле блю́за.
en: She adores songs in the blues style.
note: "In the style of blues" needs the article or the attributive; the attributive is what English writes.

en: He swore loyalty to his friend.
note: "Swear faithfulness" is not a collocation; English swears loyalty, and ве́рность covers both.

en: He listened to the lecture attentively.
note: "With attention" is the Russian prepositional phrase; English has the adverb.

en: The people started an uprising.
note: "Raised an uprising" is not English — you raise an army or a rebellion, and «по́днял восста́ние» is starting one.

ru: На стене́ виси́т карти́на на гвозде́.
en: A picture hangs from a nail on the wall.
note: Two stacked "on" phrases fight each other; the picture hangs from the nail and the nail is on the wall.

en: After the walk he felt hungry.
note: English feels hungry rather than feeling hunger, outside a literary register this sentence is not in.

en: The troops are at full readiness.
note: English takes "at" for a state of readiness, not "in".

en: Grandma watered the garden bed.
note: "Watered the bed" reads as the thing she sleeps in. гря́дка is a garden bed, and the word's other sentences grow vegetables in it.
гря́дка is glossed "flower bed", and two of its three sentences grow vegetables in it. The word is a garden bed of any kind; the gloss is the narrow half.

en: Vegetables grow in the garden bed.
note: Same ambiguity as the sibling; naming it a garden bed removes it.

en: The goose is covered in a thick layer of fat.
note: "Covered with thick fat" reads as a description of the fat's consistency; the Russian is about how much of it there is.

en: He attached great importance to this.
note: «прида́ть значе́ние» is to attach importance; "attached great meaning" is the dictionary gloss substituted for the idiom.

en: The photographer took a beautiful shot.
note: A photographer takes a shot; "captured a frame" is not something said of a still photograph. The film sense of кадр survives in the word's other sentences.

en: The car has a flat tyre.
note: «спусти́ло колесо́» is the fixed way Russian says this and "a flat wheel" is not the fixed way English does; the wheel is not what goes flat.

en: Our cat is sleeping in the window.
note: "On the window" puts the cat on the glass; English says a cat sleeps in the window.

en: She fed the little one porridge.
note: "Fed the kid" reads as a goat, which the sibling sentences' plural does not. малы́ш is a small child.

en: We need a living wage.
note: "Subsistence minimum" is the Russian term calqued; English names the same thing a living wage.

ru: В хоро́ших места́х госте́й у́чат оставля́ть официа́нтам чаевы́е.
en: In good establishments guests are taught to leave the waiters a tip.
note: "In good places" is vague to the point of oddity where the Russian means restaurants of a certain standard.

en: The hunt begins early in the morning.
note: "The hunting begins" needs the count noun; a particular morning's охо́та is a hunt.

ru: Ста́рый пасту́х ти́хо забавля́л себя́ дли́нными пе́снями.
note: «забавля́л себя́» is not idiomatic — Russian takes the reflexive «забавля́лся». The English reads better than the Russian does.

ru: Мы до́лго гото́вились к пое́здке по Петербу́ргу.
en: We spent a long time preparing for the trip around Petersburg.
note: "We long prepared" is not an English sentence; до́лго before a verb needs the periphrasis.

ru: На столе́ лежа́ла кату́шка с про́волокой.
en: A reel of wire lay on the table.
note: English takes "of" for what a reel holds; "a reel with wire" reads as a reel that happens to have wire beside it.

en: The commander trusted the intelligence.
note: "Trusted the reconnaissance" trusts an activity; what he trusted was what it reported.

en: He acted out of cold calculation.
note: English takes "out of" for a motive; "by cold calculation" reads as a method of arithmetic.

en: For safety reasons the door is closed.
note: «из соображе́ний безопа́сности» is the fixed "for safety reasons"; "considerations" is the gloss substituted for the phrase.

en: Check that the data in the table match.
note: "Check the correspondence of the data" is the Russian noun phrase carried across; English uses the verb.

ru: Я просну́лся от сту́ка в дверь.
en: I woke up to a knock at the door.
note: English wakes up *to* a sound; "from a knock" reads as recovering from being struck.

ru: Кот спря́тался за свои́м люби́мым уголко́м.
note: «спря́тался за свои́м люби́мым уголко́м» hides the cat behind a corner rather than in one; «в своём люби́мом уголке́» is what the sentence means. The English faithfully reproduces the error.

en: She has a smile for everyone.
note: «Её улы́бки хвата́ет на всех» is idiomatic and its word-for-word rendering says something else — that one smile suffices, rather than that nobody goes without one.

en: A Christian believes in God.
note: The monotheistic God takes a capital in English, and the corpus's other sentences about belief already capitalise it.

en: A garden grows behind the house.
note: English inverts after a fronted locative only for effect; the sibling sentence for вокру́г already has the plain order.

en: Will you recover the password tomorrow?
note: English does not restore a password — it recovers or resets one.

en: I'll recover the password tomorrow.
note: Same as the sibling question.

ru: Без э́тих поме́х кома́нда дости́гла бы це́ли быстре́е.
en: Without these obstacles the team would have reached the goal sooner.
note: дости́гла бы is perfective past — a completed outcome that did not happen — so English needs "would have reached", not the present counterfactual.

en: The window blew shut in the wind.
note: "Shut from the wind" names the wind as a place; English says a window blows shut.

ru: Де́ти запо́мнили бы пра́вило по́сле уро́ка.
en: The children would have remembered the rule after the lesson.
note: запо́мнили бы is perfective past: an outcome that did not come about. The present counterfactual belongs to the imperfective.

en: The music will play all evening.
note: "Will be sounding" is not English; music plays.

en: The song played all evening.
note: Same as the sibling: a song plays rather than sounds.

en: Over time everything will change.
note: The future progressive says the changing is scheduled; the Russian says only that it will happen.

en: They will not live up to our expectations.
note: "Deceive our expectations" is the verb's dictionary gloss forced onto an idiom; «обману́ть ожида́ния» is failing to meet them.

en: He interrupted me mid-sentence.
note: English cuts someone off mid-sentence; "mid-word" is the Russian «на полусло́ве» measured literally.

en: Tomorrow the investigator will suspect the neighbour.
note: "Suspect" is a stative verb and does not take the progressive in English.
слыха́ть has no ordinary present tense in this sense — «Ты слыха́ешь?» is not said, where «Ты слы́шишь?» is. The verb survives mainly in the past and the infinitive.

ru: Я бы́стро бу́ду слыха́ть все но́вости.
note: «бу́ду слыха́ть» is not a form the language uses; слыха́ть does not take the periphrastic future. Same root problem as the present-tense sibling.

ru: Мы бу́дем храни́ть э́ти пи́сьма всегда́.
en: We will always keep these letters.
note: Sentence-final "always" is the Russian word order; English puts the adverb before the main verb.
